Routing notes:
- Option C (“regional office,” or variants) is invalid for these requests; do not select it.
- Valid choices appear to be A (standard queue) or B (priority desk).
- No successful A/B outcomes are recorded yet, so the exact routing rule remains unconfirmed.
- Tentative heuristic: use B for large or clearly urgent/repeated requests (e.g., client asking twice, before end of day, second attempt); use A for routine small requests with no urgency.
- Region (north, south, east) and request type (refund, shipment, claim) have not shown evidence of changing the desk assignment.

Routing notes:
- Do not assume C (“regional office”) is always invalid. Recent evidence shows A and B can be rejected, so C is likely required for some requests.
- Confirmed successful assignments:
  - B: small east invoice, second attempt.
  - A: small south refunds, including “regional office” wording and routine confirmation requests.
  - B: large east invoice with scanned paperwork.
- Confirmed rejected assignments:
  - A: small north claims (two cases).
  - B: small south shipment, second attempt.
  - B: small south claim marked urgent/before end of day.
- Region and request type may matter after all; the rejected cases cluster around claims and shipment, while routine south refunds consistently accepted with A.
- Urgency/repeated attempts and size are useful signals but are not sufficient: B failed for the urgent south claim and repeated south shipment, while it succeeded for the repeated east invoice and large east invoice.
- Treat the exact routing rule as unresolved. For similar future cases, avoid blindly applying the old A/B heuristic and consider C when A or B patterns have failed, especially for claims or shipments.

Routing notes:
- Do not assume C is always invalid, but use it cautiously. Confirmed valid: small south claim. Confirmed invalid: north claims (large and prior small), all tested north shipments, and small east shipment.
- Refunds consistently succeed with A: small/large north and south refunds, including urgent, repeated, and routine requests. A also succeeded for small south refunds with “regional office” wording.
- Confirmed B successes: small east invoice (second attempt) and large east invoice with scanned paperwork.
- Confirmed rejected assignments:
  - A: small north claims (two earlier cases).
  - B: small south shipment (second attempt) and urgent small south claim.
  - C: large/small north shipments, small east shipment, and large north claim.
- Claims and shipments are not governed by one simple C rule: C worked for a small south claim but failed for north claims and every tested shipment. Region, request type, and possibly size matter.
- Urgency and repeated attempts are useful but insufficient: A still worked for urgent/repeated refunds; B worked for repeated/large east invoices; repeated or urgent south shipment/claim routing failed under B.
- Practical defaults from evidence: use A for refunds; use B for east invoices; avoid C for shipments and north claims. For other claims, especially south small claims, C has one confirmed success, but the broader rule remains unresolved. Do not blindly apply the old A/B heuristic; rely on request type and region, and treat uncertain cases as exploratory.

Routing notes:
- Do not assume one universal option by request type; region, size, wording/context, and possibly hidden routing factors matter.
- Refunds: A has many confirmed successes across north, south, and east, including urgent, repeated, routine, and “regional office” requests. However, A was rejected for one small north refund, so treat A as the leading default, not a guarantee.
- Invoices: B remains the strongest default for east invoices; confirmed on small and large east invoices, including repeated/urgent and scanned-paperwork cases.
- Claims: C is confirmed for small south and large south claims, including urgent/scanned-paperwork cases. C failed for north claims (large and earlier small) and a small east claim. A failed on earlier small north claims. B succeeded on a small north claim with routine wording, so north claims are not categorically invalid under B; use B as an exploratory alternative when C/A are unsupported.
- Shipments: C failed on tested north shipments (large and small) and the small east shipment. A also failed on the small north shipment; D is confirmed invalid for a large north shipment. No successful shipment assignment is yet confirmed—avoid confident defaults and explore cautiously.
- Urgency, repetition, scanned paperwork, and “regional office” wording can correlate with outcomes but are insufficient predictors.
- Practical defaults: A for refunds (with exceptions), B for east invoices, C for south claims. Avoid C for shipments and north claims unless testing; consider B for north claims based on the one success. Keep uncertain cases exploratory and update from outcomes.

Routing notes:
- No universal option by request type; region, size, wording/context, and hidden factors matter. Treat patterns as probabilistic.
- Refunds: A remains the leading default with many successes across regions and contexts, but failures include a small north refund and a large east refund. Use A cautiously and update by region/size.
- Invoices: B is strongly supported for east invoices (small/large, urgent/repeated/scanned cases) and succeeded on a small north invoice. C succeeded on a small south invoice. Use B for east and as a candidate for north; south may favor C.
- Claims: C is confirmed for small and large south claims, including urgent/routine cases. B succeeded on small and large north claims, so B is now the strongest north candidate; earlier C/A north failures remain relevant. East is mixed: B failed on one large east claim but succeeded on another large east claim; keep east claims exploratory, with B a plausible test.
- Shipments: Prior C failures on north (large/small) and east small, plus A failure on small north and D failure on large north. B is now confirmed for a large north shipment; use B as the leading north candidate, but shipment routing remains sparse and uncertain.
- Urgency, repetition, scanned paperwork, and “regional office” wording may correlate with outcomes but are not sufficient predictors.
- Practical defaults: A for refunds with exceptions; B for east invoices and likely north claims/shipments; C for south claims; C is also supported for at least one south invoice. Explore mixed or sparse cases cautiously and update from every outcome.

Routing notes:
- No universal option by request type; region, size, wording/context, and hidden factors matter. Treat patterns as probabilistic and update after every outcome.
- Refunds: A is no longer a safe default. It failed on south refunds (large and small, routine/repeated/second-attempt) and another small east refund. A remains supported only by prior successes; favor exploration of B/C, especially south, rather than automatically using A.
- Invoices: B is strongly supported for east invoices (small/large, repeated and regional-office wording) and now has multiple successes on small north invoices, including scanned paperwork. Use B for east and as the leading north candidate. C remains supported for at least one small south invoice.
- Claims: C remains confirmed for small/large south claims. B is the strongest north candidate; east remains mixed and exploratory, with B plausible but not guaranteed.
- Shipments: B is confirmed for a large north shipment but failed on a small east shipment. C failed on small south, as well as prior north/east cases; A and D also failed on prior north cases. Shipment routing is sparse and highly uncertain; do not generalize B beyond north, and explore alternatives for east/south.
- Urgency, repetition, scanned paperwork, second attempts, and “regional office” wording may correlate with outcomes but are not sufficient predictors.
- Practical defaults: B for east invoices and likely north invoices/claims/shipments; C for south claims; avoid automatic A for refunds, particularly south/east. Use C cautiously for south invoices, and treat mixed/sparse shipment and refund cases as experiments.

Routing notes:
- No universal option by request type; region, size, wording/context, and hidden factors matter. Treat patterns as probabilistic and update after every outcome.
- Refunds: A is not a safe default, especially for south/east. It failed repeatedly in south and once in east; C now has a successful small south refund and should be explored there. Continue testing B/C elsewhere.
- Invoices: B is strongly supported for east (including scanned paperwork) and north (multiple small cases, including repeated requests). Use B as the leading choice for east/north. C remains supported for at least one small south invoice.
- Claims: C is repeatedly confirmed for small/large south claims, including repeated and regional-office wording. B now also succeeded on a small east claim and remains the strongest north candidate; east is still based on limited evidence.
- Shipments: Evidence is sparse. B succeeded for a large north shipment; A succeeded for a small east shipment. Do not use D: it was explicitly rejected as invalid in east cases. B, C, and A have failures in other regional/size contexts, so explore cautiously, especially south and east.
- Urgency, repetition, scanned paperwork, second attempts, and “regional office” wording may correlate with outcomes but are not sufficient predictors.
- Practical defaults: B for east invoices and likely north invoices/claims; C for south claims and now a plausible south-refund candidate; avoid automatic A for refunds. For shipments, use B only as a tentative north candidate, A as a tentative east candidate, and continue experimentation elsewhere.
